Does the estimator work? Validation on simulated data

Source: vignettes/eventclock-validation.Rmd
eventclock-validation.Rmd
library(eventclock)
set.seed(42)

Why validate

Before trusting the Event Clock on real data, a user should know: is it biased when only about 30 daily prices are available? Are its confidence intervals right? What do the robust variants measure when news arrives in one big jump? How much does trading noise inflate it?

Real data cannot answer these questions because the true clock is unknown. Simulated data can. ec_simulate_path() draws probability paths from the package’s model (the transition law in the formula book of vignette("eventclock-brexit")) with a known clock \(A\), so any gap between estimate and truth is the estimator’s doing. Throughout, \(L = \log\{q/(1-q)\}\) are the log odds of the event probability \(q\), and the estimate is \(\widehat A = \sum (\Delta L)^2\), the sum of squared log-odds changes (method = "rv" in event_clock()).

A small helper turns a simulated path into the package’s input format:

path_to_ep <- function(p) {
  as_event_prices(
    tibble::tibble(time = as.Date("2020-01-01") + p$step, q = p$q),
    clip = c(1e-8, 1 - 1e-8)   # switch off the default [0.01, 0.99] clipping
  )
}

Bias and precision with few observations

For each window length we simulate 1000 paths with true clock \(A = 0.5\) — a typical one-month value — and compute \(\widehat A\) on each. (The vectorized sum below is exactly what event_clock(method = "rv") computes.)

A <- 0.5
reps <- 1000
grid <- c(15, 30, 60, 120, 250)
sims <- lapply(grid, function(n) {
  p <- ec_simulate_path(n_paths = reps, n_steps = n, q = 0.4, A = A)
  vapply(split(p$L, p$path), function(L) sum(diff(L)^2), numeric(1))
})
tab <- data.frame(
  n_obs = grid,
  mean = sapply(sims, mean),
  bias_pct = 100 * (sapply(sims, mean) / A - 1),
  theory_bias_pct = 100 * A / (4 * grid),
  mc_error_pct = 100 * sapply(sims, sd) / sqrt(reps) / A,
  sd = sapply(sims, sd)
)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3)
n_obs mean bias_pct theory_bias_pct mc_error_pct sd
15 0.514 2.718 0.833 1.195 0.189
30 0.506 1.162 0.417 0.834 0.132
60 0.501 0.151 0.208 0.562 0.089
120 0.500 -0.009 0.104 0.404 0.064
250 0.499 -0.132 0.050 0.287 0.045

The only systematic bias is tiny and known: given the outcome, the log odds also drift a little toward it, which adds \(A^2/(4n)\) to the expected sum — under 1% here (theory_bias_pct). The measured bias lies within about two simulation errors (mc_error_pct) of it. What short windows cost is dispersion (sd): with 30 daily observations the estimate typically misses by about a quarter of its value, which is why interval estimates matter.

Confidence intervals

event_clock(se = TRUE) adds a standard error, estimated from the sum of fourth powers of the log-odds changes, and a confidence interval built for \(\log A\) and transformed back (so it stays positive and is asymmetric). Do the intervals cover the truth as often as they claim?

coverage <- function(conf, n_steps, reps = 500, A = 0.5) {
  hits <- vapply(seq_len(reps), function(i) {
    p <- ec_simulate_path(n_paths = 1, n_steps = n_steps, q = 0.4, A = A)
    r <- event_clock(path_to_ep(p), methods = "rv", se = TRUE, conf = conf)
    r$ci_lo <= A && A <= r$ci_hi
  }, logical(1))
  mean(hits)
}
cov <- expand.grid(nominal = c(0.90, 0.95), n_obs = c(30, 60))
cov$empirical <- mapply(coverage, cov$nominal, cov$n_obs)
cov$mc_error <- 1.96 * sqrt(cov$nominal * (1 - cov$nominal) / 500)
cov
#>   nominal n_obs empirical   mc_error
#> 1    0.90    30     0.848 0.02629616
#> 2    0.95    30     0.918 0.01910372
#> 3    0.90    60     0.864 0.02629616
#> 4    0.95    60     0.950 0.01910372

Coverage is close to the nominal level, and in the shortest windows somewhat below it: with 30 observations, the 95% interval covered the truth in 91.8% of the replications, with 60 observations in 95% (mc_error is the 95% simulation band around the nominal level). In short windows, treat the intervals as slightly optimistic.

The clock does not depend on the outcome

The clock measures how much was learned, not in which direction. Paths that end with the event happening (\(J = 1\)) and paths that end without it (\(J = 0\)) carry the same expected clock:

p <- ec_simulate_path(n_paths = 400, n_steps = 60, q = 0.4, A = 0.5)
qv <- vapply(split(p$L, p$path), function(L) sum(diff(L)^2), numeric(1))
J <- vapply(split(p$J, p$path), function(j) j[1], numeric(1))
data.frame(
  outcome = c("J = 1", "J = 0"),
  mean_A_hat = c(mean(qv[J == 1]), mean(qv[J == 0])),
  n_paths = c(sum(J == 1), sum(J == 0))
)
#>   outcome mean_A_hat n_paths
#> 1   J = 1  0.5048287     152
#> 2   J = 0  0.5027828     248

Both averages sit at the true \(A = 0.5\). Constant or slowly moving risk premia therefore do not bias the clock: they change how much weight the market puts on each outcome, not how much the price moves along a given path. Premia that fluctuate day to day can add to the measured clock; ec_recovery_set() bounds that effect.

Lumpy news: what the robust variants measure

Real news is lumpy — a debate or a verdict can move the price more in one day than a month of polls. With jump_share, the simulator puts part of \(A\) into a few jump steps. Here half of the true clock (0.25) arrives in a single jump and the other half (0.25) as a smooth flow:

lumpy <- lapply(seq_len(200), function(i) {
  p <- ec_simulate_path(n_paths = 1, n_steps = 60, q = 0.4, A = 0.5,
                        jump_share = 0.5, n_jumps = 1)
  event_clock(path_to_ep(p))[, c("method", "A")]
})
agg <- do.call(rbind, lumpy)
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(A ~ method, data = agg, FUN = mean),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Mean estimate across 200 lumpy paths (true A = 0.5: 0.25 smooth + 0.25 in one jump)"
)
Mean estimate across 200 lumpy paths (true A = 0.5: 0.25 smooth + 0.25 in one jump)
method A
bipower 0.298
largest1 0.239
largest2 0.213
rv 0.527
truncated 0.236

rv recovers the total clock including the jump. truncated and largest1 land close to the smooth part (0.25): they drop the jump. bipower dampens the jump without removing it entirely and sits in between (0.298). largest2 drops one ordinary move on top of the jump and so sits a little lower than largest1. The ratio \(1 - \text{bipower}/\text{rv}\) is a simple jumpiness index, the share of the clock that came in bursts — here 0.43, against a true jump share of one half. None of the variants is wrong; they answer different questions, and comparing them is the point.

Trading noise and the sampling interval

Traded prices bounce between bid and ask on a coarse price grid. Such noise adds about twice its variance to every measured change, so the finer you sample, the more noise you add up. Here we add noise with a standard deviation of 0.04 in log odds — roughly a one-cent bounce at a price of 0.50 — to an hourly path with true clock \(A = 1\):

p <- ec_simulate_path(n_paths = 1, n_steps = 2000, q = 0.4, A = 1)
noisy <- ec_ilogit(p$L + rnorm(nrow(p), sd = 0.04))
ep_noisy <- as_event_prices(
  tibble::tibble(time = as.POSIXct("2024-01-01", tz = "UTC") +
                   3600 * p$step, q = noisy),
  clip = c(1e-8, 1 - 1e-8)
)
plot_signature(ec_signature(ep_noisy, max_every = 24)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2)

At the finest spacing the measured clock is several times the truth (dashed line); as the spacing grows it falls toward \(A = 1\). Real data show the same pattern — the hourly-versus-daily gap of the 2024 Polymarket series in vignette("eventclock-measurement"). A daily snapshot (pm_daily()) is therefore a conservative default, but it also misses genuine intraday news: report more than one sampling interval.
